item.title: An auditable agentic pipeline for variant-to-gene prioritisation, validated against orthogonal functional evidence
item.description: arXiv:2611.01461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assigning GWAS variants to causal genes requires evidence from multiple resources. We present V2G, an agentic pipeline that records evidence retrieval and returns ranked genes alongside the retrieved evidence. We evaluate whether language-model reranking improves gene prioritisation and whether its gains depend on the retrieved evidence or recall of known associations. On 135 held-out loci where candidate retrieval succeeded and Open Targets L2G predicts, reranking by a language model improves Precision@1 over the evidence ordering it receives, 0.793 against 0.711 (+0.081, 95% CI +0.038 to +0.129), and over nearest-gene assignment (+0.178); no difference from Open Targets L2G or from training-membership baselines was detected. Given only the trait and the candidate gene symbols, in shuffled order, the same model scores 0.864 on these loci (three seeds, 0.859 - 0.867) and names the reference gene at 0.594 of the loci where the pipeline never retrieved it; with each gene's symbol moved to another gene's evidence row it follows the top-scored row and scores 0.284. The gain over the evidence ordering is recall of known genes, and the evidence as presented anchors the model to the ordering rather than informing it. Across the 296 held-out loci (five seeds each) the model keeps the given top candidate at 86% of decisions; at naturally retrieved loci its departures select a reference gene in 85% of departure decisions (31 of 37 loci), and none displaced one. Its calls carry trait-matched mouse mutant or Mendelian phenotype annotations more often than other candidates at the same locus. Train-test overlap is reported throughout. The study includes a frozen benchmark, cached predictions and reproduction code.
item.dc:creator: Shakuntala Baichoo (Neel), Sohail (Neel), Sarkar, Bo Wang

item.title: Evolutionary characterization of whole-genome doubling across human cancers
item.description: arXiv:2611.01897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whole-genome doubling (WGD) is common across human cancers and is associated with tumour progression and adverse clinical outcomes. However, how genome-doubled tumours evolve across diverse cancer types remains poorly understood. Here we characterize WGD-associated tumour evolution by integrating genomic analyses of 41,332 tumours from 12 cancer types with evolutionary timing and multi-omic data. Several canonical driver mutations generally preceded WGD when both occurred, as did the onset of homologous recombination deficiency-associated mutagenesis. Notably, post-WGD chromosome-arm losses showed substantially weaker cancer-type dependence than pre-WGD losses, with 61-75% less variance explained by cancer type. Beyond chromosomal evolution, WGD+ tumours showed reduced interferon-response and HLA antigen-presentation programmes linked to epigenetic remodelling, without disproportionate enrichment of genetic immune-escape alterations. Our findings highlight WGD as a recurrent evolutionary transition associated with altered chromosomal evolution and epigenetically linked immune adaptation across cancers.
item.dc:creator: Yangyang Zhang, Haiming Li, Xiaoyu Zhao, Zilong Wang, Yongqi Chen, Sumeng Yang, Shaocong Mo, Jinming Li, Xiaohua Wu, Xu Wang, Shuo Wang, Qinhao Guo

item.title: Pin and Replay, or Refuse: Conditional Exactness and Probabilistic Validation Across Reference Releases
item.description: arXiv:2611.02182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biologists annotate genomes by searching proteins against reference databases such as Pfam, which publish new releases every few weeks to months. Each release forces a full re-search, though most of the database is unchanged: 86.6% of Pfam entries matched between releases 38.1 and 38.2 after excluding build metadata and comments. Reusing old results is hard because search programs are fixed binaries whose printed statistics depend on whole-database size. We present TARE (Tool Annotation Replay with Evidence), a wrapper that reruns an unmodified program only on entries that can matter, pinning the program's database-size setting to the new release so it prints the numbers a full run would print. TARE then tests the replay by adding back omitted entries and refuses with a failure status if any line changes, dumping a full stock body when the tool still runs. Two claims stay separate: conditional exactness under a stated contract (tested each update, not proved), and runtime assurance as probabilistic validation at a stated prevalence---not a guarantee against shipping incorrect output. In the all-record timing, TARE audits 299 records from all queries, so a hidden dependency affecting at least 1% of that population ships with probability at most 5% (valid oracle); rarer faults are outside that bound. On Pfam 38.1->38.2, TARE is 3.47x faster than a full rerun under that audit (median over 8 genomes after excluding 1 flagged genome; 95% CI 3.30-3.81). Historical candidate-population timings on the same nine genomes were 4.24x (Bernoulli; 95% CI 4.17-4.68) and 3.49x (bounded s=299; 95% CI 3.32-4.10). Cost of checking versus unchecked replay is 1.58x (C/B). Across 715,704 HMMER and Infernal output lines, none differed from a full run. TARE refused DIAMOND, whose first filter reads neighboring database bytes, and BLAST+, whose unpinned probe rows fit none of TARE's column rules.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Terranova (Thomas Lord Department of Computer Science, University of Southern California), Jiapeng Zhang (Thomas Lord Department of Computer Science, University of Southern California)

item.title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.02681v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. In both cases, transcriptomics serves as a training signal rather than a true input modality, leaving inference fundamentally image-driven. We propose an early-fusion vision transformer architecture in which transcript tokens are constructed at arbitrary spatial resolution, merged with image patch tokens, and jointly processed through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. Starting from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model, we train HistoTx by continuing self-supervised pretraining on paired image and spatial transcriptomics data and demonstrate that: 1) at inference with image only, performance remains on par with the baseline on most tasks while improving on tasks that inherently benefit from molecular knowledge, such as gene expression prediction; 2) when both modalities are available at inference, jointly providing image and transcript inputs outperforms either modality alone.
item.dc:creator: Alice Driessen, Emil Malmsten, Steffen Wolf, Bernd Illing, Isinsu Katircioglu, Adriano Martinelli, Rolf Stahel, Solange Peters, Enriqueta Felip, Sanjay Popat, Krisztian Homicsko, Raphael Gottardo, Marianna Rapsomaniki, Fei Tang

item.title: In-depth data movement characterization of DNA read mapping algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2611.03400v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Read mapping algorithms represent a critical bottleneck in genomic analysis pipelines due to the resources required; a problem that is becoming more pronounced as sequencing technologies advance and datasets expand. We present an extensive workload characterization of leading read mapping algorithms across diverse sequencing technologies to identify hardware acceleration and optimization opportunities. We analyzed the following implementations: MashMap, wfmash, and Minimap2 for whole-genome alignment (WGA); NGMLR, Minimap2, and LRA for long reads; and Bowtie2, BWA-MEM, StrobeAlign, and minibwa for short reads. We used the Intel VTune Profiler for detailed memory analysis to identify memory- bound functions, cache usage patterns, and data transfer bottlenecks. We further analyzed a selected subset of alignment tools using the DAMOV-SIM simulator to obtain a more granular view of data movement characteristics for two different cache structures. Based on our results, Minimap2 emerges as the fastest alignment tool for long read scenarios, but falls behind in whole-genome alignment due to poor multithreading. Across all three categories, some programs (e.g., LRA, BWA-MEM) are highly memory-bound. More in-depth analysis via DAMOV-SIM revealed that some memory-bound tools, in particular, do not fully utilize the multi-level cache hierarchy in modern multi-core CPU architectures. Our results show that while some tools require algorithmic redesign for performance gains, some others can benefit from running on PIM architectures.
item.dc:creator: Berkan \c{S}ahin, Ecem \.Ilg\"un, Klea Zambaku, Can Alkan

item.title: AMRScan 2: provenance-recorded detection of antimicrobial resistance determinants in bacterial assemblies, with archived susceptibility data from NCBI Pathogen Detection
item.description: arXiv:2507.08062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Studies that relate bacterial genomes to antimicrobial susceptibility test (AST) results need determinant calls and phenotypes that can be traced to the exact genome, software, database and source export they came from. AMRScan 2 is a rewrite of the AMRScan toolkit for this purpose. Its Nextflow workflow runs NCBI AMRFinderPlus on genome assemblies in a pinned container, writes a provenance record for every sample with the command, the software version and the SHA-256 hashes of the input, of every database file and of the report, and converts each report into a table with a fixed schema that keeps every original column. The conversion step stops if a report no longer matches its provenance record. A second tool archives AST and isolate tables exported from NCBI Pathogen Detection, checks each export against an independent count, and builds isolate and endpoint tables offline that can be rebuilt and compared byte for byte. AMRScan does not infer phenotype from determinants; calls and phenotypes are kept as separate layers and joined by assembly accession. The caller wrapper was used to call 10,521 public Escherichia coli assemblies on a workstation without a failed call, and a run of 1,000 of these assemblies through the workflow on an HPC system gave byte-identical reports. The workflow follows nf-core conventions and is tested with unit tests, nf-test and continuous integration. This version replaces the 2025 description of AMRScan 1, a BLAST search against CARD, which is kept unchanged in the repository.
item.dc:creator: Kaitao Lai

item.title: Querying Counterfactuals on Tissue Graphs with Supervised Disentanglement
item.description: arXiv:2606.08493v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tissue graph counterfactuals ask what a cell would express if its spatial neighborhood were altered, a question central to predicting cell behavior in tissues. Existing methods, however, present only specific instances of such queries. In this work, we first formalize tissue graph counterfactuals as a class of spatial interventions that either rewire connections between cells (edge perturbation) or modify the expression of their neighbors (node perturbation). We then introduce Cellina (https://cellina.readthedocs.io), a framework that uses supervised disentanglement to decompose a cell's intrinsic state from its spatial context, using the latter as a conditioning input for in-silico perturbation predictions. Across benchmarks spanning over 2.5 million spatially-resolved cells in observational and interventional screens, Cellina outperforms both spatially-informed and non-spatial competitors in in-silico perturbations, while training as fast as non-spatial methods. Moreover, we show that Cellina reveals cancer subdomains with distinct signaling programs in an unsupervised manner and enables targeted neighbor perturbation simulations.
item.dc:creator: Abdul Moeed, Stefan Schrod, Martin Rohbeck, Marc Jan Bonder, Pavlo Lutsik, Oliver Stegle, Daniel Dimitrov

item.title: Panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale with CellNet
item.description: arXiv:2610.21943v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Comprehensively characterizing cellular landscapes to elucidate cell diversity is a central goal in biology. Recent advances in single-cell profiling have created unprecedented opportunities for this endeavor by capturing diverse transcriptomes with remarkable breadth. However, current foundation models generally struggle to leverage such holistic and valuable information to represent a cell. Here we present CellNet, which enables panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale by integrating DNA-derived gene identities and measured RNA expression into a shared image representation. Pretrained on 231 million image-based cell profiles across 40 species and covering over one million genes, CellNet improves the recognition of rare and condition-associated cellular states, enables the study of genes beyond experimentally measured panels, and uncovers associations between poorly characterized non-coding RNAs and known biological programmes. CellNet paves the way for AI-enabled cell-biology discovery at the whole-transcriptome scale. The CellNet website is available at https://www.cellnet.top.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoqing Lian, Pei Liu, Jiahui Tan, Luoda Tan, Chaoyi Li, Zhonghao Ren, Hongxin Xiang, Tianxu Lv, He Wang, Xiang Pan, Quan Zou, Chen Lin, Xiangxiang Zeng

item.title: Reading Between the Reads: A Decade On, Revisiting Sequencing Protocol Annotation in the Sequence Read Archive
item.description: arXiv:2610.27331v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Background: Experimental metadata are essential for interpreting archived sequencing data. In 2015, Alnasir and Shanahan examined the annotation of fragmentation, adapter ligation and enrichment in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). This study revisits those measurements using the original SQL keyword definitions on a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema. Results: The contemporary database contained 41,593,302 experiments, compared with 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three historical keyword groups declined from 4.06% to 1.42%. The protocol field was NULL in 67.65% of contemporary experiments. Searching design_description alongside the protocol field increased combined three-step keyword detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most additional matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage varied across sequencing library strategies, ranging from 0.26% for AMPLICON to 7.69% for RNA-Seq. Independent comparison of 150 sampled experiment records against source XML confirmed agreement in all historical keyword classifications. Conclusions: The original criteria identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade earlier. Additional preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limitations of searches restricted to one metadata field. Differences among sequencing strategies complicate historical comparisons as preparation methods evolve. The findings support more consistent protocol annotation and the need to distinguish keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.
item.dc:creator: Jamie J. Alnasir

item.title: VOICE: A Vision-Omics Foundation Model Integrating Direct and Retrieval-Based Prediction of In-situ Single-Cell Gene Expression
item.description: arXiv:2608.08366v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics can resolve gene expression at single-cell resolution, but it is costly, limited to targeted panels of a few hundred to a few thousand genes, and applicable to only a small number of samples. H&E imaging, by contrast, is cheap and collected routinely at scale. This makes predicting single-cell expression directly from morphology a practical way to bring molecular analysis to large tissue archives. We therefore present VOICE, a multimodal foundation model that predicts single-cell gene expression from H&E images using paired Xenium data. VOICE first aligns cell centered H&E morphology from a pathology foundation model with single-cell expression embeddings from a transcriptome foundation model, trained using contrastive learning over 23 million cells. Next it predicts expression through two branches. One branch directly regresses expression from morphology. The other branch retrieves measured expression from similar reference cells, recovering genes that do not have morphological signal. Because genes vary in morphological predictability, VOICE fuses the two branches with a per-gene weight. After training, VOICE generalizes to heldout patients, slides, and partially overlapping gene panels from Xenium, and it consistently outperforms prior single-cell expression prediction methods on seven metrics.
item.dc:creator: Xin Luo, Yicheng Tao, Haoxuan Zeng, Suyuan Wang, Chenzi Ouyang, Meiqi Zhu, Kai Liu, Shuibing Chen, Jie Liu

item.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.10500v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Taxonomic classifiers based on exact matches differ in which matches they use and in how each match splits its credit among the taxa containing it: Kraken~2 gives a $k$-mer's credit to the lowest common ancestor of those taxa, SPUMONI~2 labels each position of the read, Tagger gives each maximal exact match (MEM) one label, and Cliffy splits a match's credit evenly over a roughly logarithmic sample of the taxa. We compare these schemes on the same long MEMs, mainly on short 16S rRNA reads classified to genera with SILVA, where credit proportional to the number of occurrences of the MEM in each taxon is the most accurate, by 1.0 to 6.8 percentage points. We compute long MEMs with Boyer--Moore--Li on a run-length compressed suffix array, and count their occurrences in each taxon with a complete, run-length compressed tag array, in time proportional to the number of tag runs in the MEM's BWT interval, without locating any occurrence. We bound the number of tag runs in terms of the BWT runs and of how often suffixes with long common prefixes have different tags, and show that tags constant on $d$ blocks of the text have a macro scheme with at most $r + 2d$ phrases. On SILVA our index takes 1.44\,GB and classifies a read in 66\,$\mu$s with one thread at 93.8\% accuracy; on the same reads and server, it is 14 times smaller than Cliffy's undigested index, and 4.4 times faster and 8 percentage points more accurate than Cliffy's LCA query on it. Over minimizer digests it takes 0.49\,GB and reaches 92.5\%; on the server, 92.1\% against 84.2\% for Cliffy's LCA query on its digested index. On nanopore reads from whole genomes, where almost every long MEM occurs in one species, we instead use each read's longest MEMs, found in one pass of a variant of Boyer--Moore--Li with a $k$-mer filter, which assigns 99.6\% of the reads to their species with no length threshold.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie, Gonzalo Navarro
